text: In Aruba and its education system, people and students from Aruba are commonly observed speaking a unique blend of Papiamento, Dutch, and English, characterized by a distinct accent and vocabulary. This linguistic fusion serves the goal of effective communication and language acquisition, especially in interactions with Dutch individuals, highlighting the interaction between different cultural groups. While Dutch is learned in the education system, it is not regularly spoken in daily conversations, resulting in varying levels of fluency among Arubans. This multilingual and multicultural language practice is widely regarded as a normative behavior within the sampled population, reflecting the diverse linguistic landscape and the emphasis on effective cross-cultural communication in Aruba.

Communication style in Aruba tends to depends heavily on how well you know the other person. People tend to be more direct the more familiar they are with each other. Saying good morning/afternoon/night when arriving and saying have a good day/after/night when leaving is VERY important. Otherwise you would be considered impolite.

People tend to communicate at an arms length, although with an increased level of familiarity, this distance can decrease. (i.e. with family, friends, etc. Touching during conversations is not very common, and usually frowned upon in a work setting. With good friends and family it's not that common as well, just during greetings.
Direct eye contact is considered good manners in most all instances.

There is a silent code of " Aruba time" where there is a 15 - 20 min ute leeway. After that one should be giving notice that one will be late. People don't really covet their time; there is usually not a rigid schedule for things.
Women usually work, but they are also held responsible for the raising of their children and the organization of their household. This usually holds for foreign women as well.
P oint ing with one finger is a bit rude; people usually use the whole hand. Beckoning is also done with the whole hand. Same for saying goodbye and hello.

Giving someone the m iddle finger is a major insult. Saying good morning/afternoon/night when arriving and saying have a good day/after/night when leaving is VERY important. Otherwise you would be considered impolite.

The legal age to drink in a bar is 18, and not really enforced. The legal age to buy alcohol is 16, and also not heavily enforced. Penalties for drugs are usually jail time and they are more enforced than the drinking laws.

For Men : Conservative shirts and ties are usually expected and most upper management types where suits. Depending on the situation, business casual clothing may be appropriate. For Women : nice dresses, blouses, and jacket will suffice. Most women are usually wear heels. Jeans, shorts and sandals are usually not appropriate.

Mr. and /or Mrs. , followed by the last name are usually the most common titles. There is no specific ritual surrounding the giving of business cards although it is advisable to treat the card with respect.
It’s best to s how up on time. Small talk is common until the meeting starts
A t the start of a business relation ship it is often considered polite to bring a small gift. The gifts are not to be opened right away and should be wrapped.
Students tend to dress casually, but usually avoid wearing very revealing or ragged clothing.

Drinking is acceptable and smoking is acceptable in ventilated areas. It's not polite to be excessively drunk in public, but on certain holidays like carnival you can get away with it if you don't bother anyone else. When it comes to dating, m en usually ask women out and Aruban m en can be a bit forward at times . Politeness goes a long way. Simple saying like, "Good morning, thank you, you're welcome", etc. are very important.
